sections.title: 听力 A · 13—16
sections.transcript: Our village mobile cinema began after the nearest theatre closed. At first, films were shown in the sports hall on Friday evenings. Audiences liked the large screen but complained that the plastic chairs were uncomfortable. We now use the community centre, where seats are better and heating costs less. Tickets can be bought online, yet we keep twenty at the door for residents without internet access. Last month a projector problem delayed the film for forty minutes. Instead of sending everyone home, a local musician performed, and many people asked us to invite her again. We therefore plan a short live performance before one film each month. The cinema is run by volunteers, but ticket income covers film licences and equipment. Our next aim is to offer an afternoon programme for families during school holidays. sections.title: 听力 A · 17—20
sections.transcript: When I bought a telescope, I expected to see colourful pictures like those in books. My first view of Jupiter was a tiny pale circle, and I felt disappointed. Then I joined a local astronomy club. Its leader advised me to begin with the moon because its details are easier to recognise. She also taught me to let my eyes adjust to darkness instead of looking repeatedly at my phone. The club meets in a field outside town, but cloudy evenings are not wasted. Members discuss photographs, repair equipment, or plan future observations indoors. I once assumed expensive equipment produced the best experience. Now I know patience and knowledge matter more. Last spring I helped a child find Saturn for the first time. Her excitement reminded me why sharing the sky can be more rewarding than observing alone. The experience also showed that careful planning matters whenever people make decisions about learning astronomy. sections.transcript: Welcome to the Hill Farm volunteer weekend. The project began in 2016 to protect traditional fruit trees. This Saturday we will meet at the red barn at nine thirty. Please do not wait at the farmhouse, which is private. Our main task is to measure young apple trees and record their condition. Each group will receive a clipboard and a blue measuring tape. Lunch is provided, including a vegetarian soup, but volunteers should bring their own cup. Wear strong shoes because the grass may be wet. At two o'clock, farm manager Rosa King will demonstrate how to plant a tree safely. The day ends at four, and a free bus leaves for the station fifteen minutes later. sections.title: 阅读 A · 26—30
sections.text: When Maya moved into an old house, she needed a drill for one small repair. Buying one seemed wasteful, so she joined a tool library. Members pay a modest annual fee and borrow equipment for several days. At first Maya worried that shared tools would be unreliable. In fact, every item was checked when returned, and volunteers demonstrated safe use. The library also offered short workshops. During one session, Maya learned that her shelf problem required different wall plugs rather than a stronger drill. This advice prevented damage and saved time. The project faces challenges: popular tools must be booked, and late returns affect other members. Organisers therefore send reminders and ask borrowers to report faults honestly. Maya still owns basic hand tools, but she no longer believes every household needs rarely used equipment. For her, the library provides access, practical knowledge, and a chance to meet neighbours who enjoy solving problems. sections.title: 阅读 A · 31—35
sections.text: University student Owen typed every lecture because he could record more words that way. Yet before examinations, his notes felt unfamiliar. He remembered copying sentences but not thinking about them. A tutor suggested handwriting one lecture each week. Owen initially disliked the slower pace. Soon he found that he had to select key ideas and express them briefly. That decision-making helped him understand relationships between concepts. Handwriting was not ideal for everything. Names, dates, and quotations could be captured more accurately on a laptop, while diagrams were easier on paper. Owen developed a mixed system: he typed factual details and later drew a one-page summary by hand. The process took extra time after class, but revision became faster because the summary revealed what he did not understand. He does not argue that handwriting is naturally superior. The useful change was moving from passive recording to active selection. Students should choose a method according to the material and purpose, then test whether it actually helps them remember and explain ideas. sections.title: 阅读 A · 36—40
sections.text: Residents of Pine Valley once believed brighter streets always meant safer streets. When the council proposed downward-facing lamps, some feared the roads would become dark. Engineers explained that old globe-shaped lights sent much of their light upward or into bedroom windows. The new design directed light onto pavements, where it was needed. A three-month trial began on two streets. Measurements showed lower electricity use, while residents reported that faces and obstacles were easier to see because there was less glare. Amateur astronomers welcomed the darker sky, but they were not the only beneficiaries. Several people slept better after harsh light stopped entering their rooms, and insects gathered in smaller numbers around the lamps. Not everyone was satisfied: one shopkeeper wanted his sign illuminated all night. The council allowed limited lighting until closing time. The trial showed that reducing wasted light does not necessarily reduce useful light. Good design can improve visibility while saving energy and protecting nighttime conditions, although local needs still require discussion. The experience also showed that careful planning matters whenever people make decisions about dark-sky lighting. chart.title: 学生每周课外阅读时间

questions.prompt: Write an essay of about 120 words based on the chart. Describe and interpret the chart briefly, and give your comments.
questions.explanation: 先概括总体趋势和关键数据，再解释可能原因，最后提出自己的看法或建议；避免只逐项抄写数字。

sections.model: The chart shows how many hours per week students spent reading for pleasure between 2021 and 2025. The figure rose from 2.1 hours in 2021 to 3.6 hours in 2025, with growth in every year. This steady increase may reflect easier access to school libraries and digital books. In my view, reading for pleasure is valuable because it improves language ability while also helping students relax. Schools can support the habit by offering varied books rather than requiring everyone to read the same title. They might also provide a short quiet reading period each week. However, the goal should not be to compete over numbers. Students are more likely to continue reading when they can choose material that truly interests them.
